Chapter 1: Growing Up in a World Shaped by Fear and Reverence
Imagine waking up every morning to the same song, with the same faces watching you from every wall. Childhood, in a place like this, feels different. It’s not about giggles and games, or the familiar comfort of family—it’s about the constant gaze of something much bigger.
Loyalty isn’t just encouraged. It’s everything. And if you ever let doubt sneak in? Well, that’s a risk few are willing to take.
Picture a young boy in a classroom, his eyes drawn to two portraits hanging above the chalkboard. These aren’t just leaders—they’re more like the sun and the moon, always present, always watching. The teacher’s voice, soft yet unyielding, spins tales of sacrifice and brilliance. Gratitude isn’t just a nice idea here; it’s what keeps you safe.
Back home, the atmosphere changes but the tension lingers. Parents speak so quietly, almost as if every wall might have ears. A careless word? That could mean trouble for everyone.
Kids learn early on that their lives aren’t really their own. Even the smallest mistake—a missed bow, a question that’s a little too bold—can raise suspicion. There’s always this sense that someone, somewhere, is listening in. Sure, there’s a strong sense of community, but it’s woven from caution as much as from hope.
As the boy gets older, he starts to see things differently. He’s taught to fear the world beyond his borders, to see outsiders as threats, and to believe that his nation’s founder is larger than life. Every book he reads, every song he sings, every joke he hears—they’re all carefully chosen to send the same message: trust what you’re told, and love your leader above all else.
But underneath, cracks begin to show. Maybe a neighbor vanishes without a trace. Maybe a friend’s family is suddenly gone, leaving behind an empty, silent home. People whisper, but never too loudly. The true fear isn’t just punishment; it’s being labeled disloyal. That’s a mark no one wants.
In a place like this, figuring out who you really are gets tricky. People wear masks. They hide their real thoughts—even from themselves sometimes. The line between what you believe and what you pretend to believe? It gets blurry. For some, it’s just normal life. But for others, it’s the beginning of something quietly rebellious.
Control here isn’t just about rules and punishments. It’s in your mind, in the stories you hear at school, the songs you sing at rallies, the rituals you follow every day. It’s a world where love and fear are so tangled up, you can hardly tell them apart. And maybe, just maybe, the bravest thing you can do is to picture a life that’s different.
